library(stockplotr)

Integrated assessment models such as FIMS and Stock Synthesis are fit to many data sources at once, including landings and fishery and survey indices of abundance. {stockplotr} has a set of diagnostic plots for these fits that work the same way for each model. They are based on the figures from r4ss and on diagnostics from JABBA and ss3diags.

Diagnostic Function What it shows Equivalent in other packages
Data availability plot_data_availability() Which data are available for each fleet and year r4ss: SSplotData()
Index fit plot_index_fit() Observed indices with intervals and the expected index r4ss: SSplotIndices() subplots 2 and 5
Observed vs. expected plot_index_obs_exp() Whether indices are proportional to modeled abundance r4ss: SSplotIndices() subplots 3 and 6
All indices plot_index_overlay() Conflicting trends among indices r4ss: SSplotIndices() subplot 9
Landings fit plot_landings_fit() Observed and expected landings r4ss: SSplotCatch()
Runs tests plot_runs_test() Non-random residuals and outliers ss3diags: SSplotRunstest(); JABBA
Joint residuals plot_joint_residuals() Patterns shared among fleets, and RMSE ss3diags: SSplotJABBAres(); JABBA

Input data

Each function takes the output of a model directly:

  • FIMS: the output of FIMS::get_estimates() (on its own or passed through convert_output()), or the FIMSFit object itself. FIMS reports years as indices (1 = first model year), so use start_year to label the x-axis with years.
  • Stock Synthesis: the output of convert_output(), or the list returned by r4ss::SS_output().
  • Other models: the output of convert_output(), or a tidy data frame (see ?prepare_fit_data).

Indices and landings are first reshaped with prepare_fit_data(), which returns the observed and expected values, the observation error, and the residuals. Call it directly to inspect the data behind any of the plots:

fits <- prepare_fit_data(example_data)
head(fits)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 11
#>   data_type fleet      year observed expected    se distribution used  residual
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>        <lgl>    <dbl>
#> 1 index     Triennial  1980    1835     3323. 0.381 log_normal   TRUE   -0.594 
#> 2 index     Triennial  1983    1968.    2438. 0.343 log_normal   TRUE   -0.214 
#> 3 index     Triennial  1986    1819.    2212. 0.345 log_normal   TRUE   -0.196 
#> 4 index     Triennial  1989    2590.    2178. 0.338 log_normal   TRUE    0.173 
#> 5 index     Triennial  1992    1861.    1933. 0.339 log_normal   TRUE   -0.0384
#> 6 index     Triennial  1995    2071.    2517. 0.350 log_normal   TRUE   -0.195 
#> # i 2 more variables: std_residual <dbl>, loglike <dbl>

The examples below use the Stock Synthesis model in example_data. The same calls work for FIMS; for example, with the FIMS example model:

data("estimates_big_optimized", package = "FIMS")
fims <- estimates_big_optimized
plot_data_availability(fims, start_year = 2001)
plot_index_fit(fims, start_year = 2001)
plot_runs_test(fims, data_type = c("index", "landings"), start_year = 2001)

What data are in the model?

plot_data_availability(example_data)

Point sizes are relative within each data type: landings by the amount landed and indices by their precision (1 / SE).

Fits to indices and landings

plot_index_fit(example_data)

plot_index_fit(example_data, log = TRUE)

Indices with lognormal errors are often easier to judge on a log scale, where the intervals are symmetric. Plotting observed against expected values shows whether the index is proportional to the modeled abundance; a smoother with a slope less than one suggests hyperstability:

plot_index_obs_exp(example_data)

Plotting all indices relative to their means shows whether they tell the same story:

plot_index_overlay(example_data)

Landings are usually fit closely; large residuals indicate a problem.

plot_landings_fit(example_data)

Residual diagnostics

Runs tests

The runs test checks whether residuals are randomly positive and negative over time, and the three-sigma control limits flag outliers (Carvalho et al. 2017). The shaded band is green when the test passes and red when the residuals are not random:

plot_runs_test(example_data)

Here the last Triennial survey observation (2004) is outside the control limits.

Joint residuals

Plotting the residuals of all fleets together, as in JABBA, shows years in which all data sources are above or below the model, and the root-mean-square error (RMSE) summarizes the overall fit:

plot_joint_residuals(example_data)

References

Carvalho, F., Punt, A.E., Chang, Y.-J., Maunder, M.N., and Piner, K.R. 2017. Can diagnostic tests help identify model misspecification in integrated stock assessments? Fisheries Research 192: 28-40.

Carvalho, F., et al. 2021. A cookbook for using model diagnostics in integrated stock assessments. Fisheries Research 240: 105959.

Winker, H., Carvalho, F., and Kapur, M. 2018. JABBA: Just Another Bayesian Biomass Assessment. Fisheries Research 204: 275-288.
